newsitem.title: UK: POLL-Volatile stg key obstacle to EMU membership.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Volatile stg key obstacle to EMU membership.

text.p: Sterling has fought its way back up to the levels it failed to hold in the EU's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) five years ago but the currency remains too volatile for membership of any fixed exchange rate regime, analysts say.

A Reuters poll of 18 economists shows that Britain will meet the criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU) on the size of its budget deficit, total debt, inflation and long-term interest rates, yet fails conspicuously on a fifth requirement -- currency stability.
Since August last year sterling has rocketed by 31 percent against the deutschemark -- the anchor currency for EMU -- and is now back its old ERM central parity of 2.95.

But analysts argue that such a mammoth gain is unlikely to be the harbinger of a new era of steady exchange rates and accordingly not one contributor to a second Reuters poll published on Wednesday, of 33 economists, believes the UK will be part of the single European currency at its inception in 1999.
"What really matters is not the actual level of the currency, it's stability and that is what sterling is clearly lacking," said Gerlof de Vrij, senior bond strategist at ABN-AMRO in Amsterdam.
But sterling does have one factor which could mean it is more resilient at around 3.0 marks than when it was in the ERM -- the foreign exchange market itself has marshalled its gains.
"A level of 2.95 (marks) is probably more sustainable now than it was in 1992. The pound has got here as a free-floating currency -- before it was dictated by governments, not markets," he said.

In 1992, massive speculative selling meant that even huge hikes in official interest rates, up to 15 percent, could not keep the pound within its 6.0 percent fluctuation bands. It was forced to quit the system altogether and suffered a 10 percent devaluation. A year later the ERM itself fell apart.
Part of the reason for sterling's rout from the ERM was the perception that the British interest rate and economic cycles were out of synch with those of continental Europe.

Then the enormous stimulus from German reunification demanded high interest rates to prevent an unsustainable boom on the continent. But for Britain, real interest rates around six percent during its ERM membership, spelt the longest recession since World War Two.
Britain only emerged from the recession once the pound left the ERM and rates came down.
Analysts warn that Britain is still out of kilter with the European bloc and the chances are slender for a period of tranquility on the foreign exchanges.
Financial markets believe Britain's official 7.0 percent interest rates are now close to their peak, after four rises since May to keep a lid on burgeoning consumer demand.
But in Germany, by contrast, they are beginning to turn their thoughts to higher rates after no change for more than a year.

"There is potential for a correction in the deutschemark next year and also for an independent correction to sterling as the interest rate cycle reaches its peak," said Yamaichi chief economist John Shepperd.

Shepperd argues that sterling would look more competitive at around 2.50-2.60 marks and that the recent strength of sterling will gradually begin to undermine Britain's trade position as goods become too expensive for foreign buyers.
Moreover the rate of 2.95 marks could hardly be viewed an auspicious one. "We got stuffed in at 2.95 last time and I think having the same rate again might be a bit of a psychological hurdle."

The other crucial difficulty for Britain is the absence of a political will to be a part of a single currency. "The main problem is that public opinion is so anti-EMU," said Banque Paribas EMU economist Sharda Persaud.

"There's cross party support for a referendum before any decision to join is taken and whether Britain will ever be part of a single currency largely depends on how successful the first few years are."

Persaud also argues that much of sterling's strength is down to the very perception that it will not be involved with EMU and is therefore a safe haven from possible future turmoil amid increasing speculation that the convergence criteria will be fudged to allow a broader membership base from the start.
"People are assuming that EMU will be a soft currency. That means they would rather hold sterling and dollars."
